---
title: "Benford First-Digit Analysis of Provincial Vote Totals"
author: "Cameron Batts"
output: html_document
---

## Problem
Compare the first digits of 30 reported provincial vote totals with an explicit Benford reference distribution.

## Approach
Parse comma-separated vote totals as numeric, validate positive integer counts and compare all nine first-digit frequencies with log10(1+1/d). Retain the chi-square approximation and add a proposed fixed-null Monte Carlo calculation for small expected counts.

## Verified findings
Independent Python calculation reproduced first-digit counts [5, 4, 5, 3, 2, 4, 3, 1, 3], Pearson χ²=7.5941 (8 degrees of freedom), and the approximate p-value 0.4741. Seven of nine expected digit counts are below five; the smallest is about 1.37.

## Limitations
The asymptotic p-value needs caution because of small expected counts. Non-rejection does not prove conformity, and neither conformity nor deviation establishes election integrity. Population and turnout constrain provincial totals, and the appropriateness of the Benford reference model requires justification. The original repository did not document the upstream election-data source.

## Data
Data/Election2009Iran.csv contains 30 provincial rows. Only Total votes is used for the reported test; candidate names and regional labels remain factual source data.

## Verification
Counts and relevant numerical findings were checked independently in Python. The revised R workflow was executed and rendered during this pass. Historical images are retained separately from the revised workflow.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
project_root <- if (dir.exists("Data")) "." else ".."
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(project_root))
```
```{r data}
votes <- read.csv("Data/Election2009Iran.csv", check.names = FALSE)
raw <- votes[["Total votes"]]
totals <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", as.character(raw), fixed = TRUE))
stopifnot(length(totals) == 30, all(is.finite(totals)), all(totals > 0),
          all(totals == floor(totals)))
first <- as.integer(substr(format(totals, scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE), 1, 1))
counts <- table(factor(first, levels = 1:9))
expected_probability <- log10(1 + 1/(1:9))
comparison <- data.frame(digit = 1:9, observed = as.integer(counts),
                         expected = length(totals) * expected_probability)
comparison
```

## Goodness-of-fit checks
```{r tests}
# Approximation is retained for comparison, with the expected-count warning visible.
asymptotic <- chisq.test(counts, p = expected_probability)
asymptotic
# Fixed-null multinomial simulation avoids relying on the chi-square asymptotic approximation.
set.seed(42)
simulated <- chisq.test(counts, p = expected_probability, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 100000)
simulated
barplot(rbind(comparison$observed / length(totals), expected_probability),
        beside = TRUE, names.arg = 1:9, legend.text = c("Observed", "Benford"),
        ylab = "First-digit proportion")
```
The first-digit model is an assumed reference distribution. Provincial totals are constrained by population and turnout; agreement or disagreement is not a reliable standalone verdict about election integrity. The small sample also limits sensitivity. The simulated result above is a proposed R calculation and has not been executed in this update.

## Method reference
Deckert, Myagkov and Ordeshook (2011), *Benford's Law and the Detection of Election Fraud*, Political Analysis, doi:10.1093/pan/mpr014. This research discusses limitations of Benford tests for elections.


## Validation update - October 22, 2026
The revised R Markdown executed and rendered on 30 provincial totals. Chi-square statistic=7.5941; asymptotic p=0.4741; fixed-null multinomial simulation p=0.4643 with 100,000 replicates and seed 42. Sparse expected counts limit the asymptotic test. This does not prove either fraud or absence of fraud.

Fresh outputs are recorded in Reports/validation_results.json. Archived source results use different preprocessing where noted.
